America’s cattle herd is near its smallest size since 1951 [File: Jack Dura/AP Photo]By Meg DuffPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
In late August, United States President Donald Trump announced a 90-day pause on certain beef tariffs, making beef cheaper to import, particularly from Brazil.
That decision was framed as a way to bring down prices for consumers, but it landed as a betrayal for many US ranchers, who were getting ready to take their cattle to market.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4‘Foreign policy is the economy’: How Iran war is shaping US midterm votelist 2 of 4Why Chinese families are rushing to buy goldlist 3 of 4Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaskalist 4 of 4Trump’s broken promises: economy, war and ICEend of list
It is too soon to tell how the decision will ultimately affect grocery prices, but the impact on ranchers was immediate: prices at cattle auctions plummeted, temporarily lowering ranchers’ profits. The United States Cattlemen’s Association, the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association and the Farm Bureau, all member organisations that represent ranchers, opposed the decision.
Rural Republican members of Congress also distanced themselves, but it is not yet clear how ranchers will vote in the midterms — or whether those votes will decide races.
Chad Basinger, a rancher in Pretty Prairie, Kansas, is sceptical that the imports will have a significant impact.
“I know there’s people that have said, ‘Well I’m just gonna vote for the other party’ or ‘I’m not gonna vote’ or ‘This administration’s really let me down’. So yes, there will be people that swing the other way in the midterms. But overall I don’t think it’ll be that much,” Basinger said.

Mourners carry the body of one of three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike on the Islamic University building on October 25, 2026 [AFP]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
At least seven Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza, including one that targeted a university campus in Gaza City.
Three security guards were killed in an Israeli air strike on the Islamic University campus on Sunday, the second attack that targeted the institution in the space of a few hours.

Reporting from the scene immediately after the attack, Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud said, “The aftermath was massive.”
“The bloodstains, the pieces of flesh of the bodies that were torn apart were on the ground; the smell of the acrid, burning concrete mixed with the flesh and the blood,” Mahmoud added, saying that the Al Jazeera team had just finished filming on site and greeted the three security guards before the strike killed them.
“We could hear the hissing sound of flying shrapnel everywhere to the point we thought we were going to be hit,” our correspondent said.
In the earlier drone strike on the campus, seven female students were injured by flying shrapnel.
“One of them was seriously injured and was transferred to a nearby field hospital,” Mahmoud said.

A coffin is lowered during the funeral on Sunday for victims of the church shooting in Karak in Jordan [Alaa Al Sukhni/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Thousands of mourners have gathered for the funerals of eight of the victims of a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan, with Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also in attendance.
The burials on Sunday were beside St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, southwest of the capital, Amman, two days after attackers opened fire during another funeral there.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?list 2 of 2Jordan’s King Abdullah orders firm response after deadly church attackend of list
Nine people were killed and dozens wounded in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority, prompting three days of national mourning.
The ninth victim, Mohammed al-Qasous, is due to be buried on Monday, his family told the AFP news agency.
Coffins wrapped in Jordanian flags were carried through crowds gathered around the church in Karak province, as priests led prayers and security personnel stood guard.
Prime Minister Hassan attended the service alongside government ministers and senior military and civilian officials, according to Jordan’s state news agency, Petra.
Thousands of citizens also participated in the funeral procession, Petra said.
Among those caught in Friday’s shooting was Sahar al-Halsa, who told the Reuters news agency from her nearby home that she sheltered behind a pillar as gunfire erupted and people screamed.
When she rushed outside, she found her cousin Assem lying wounded.

Protesters fly a French flag amid clashes in Paris on Saturday [Reuters/Abdul Saboor]By Caolán MageePublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe.
Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.

Continued disruption to energy supplies is pushing up household costs as winter in Europe approaches, adding fuel to protests over living standards that have engulfed European capitals in recent weeks.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Sunday drew attention to what he described as a shift in Germany’s position on attacks against Iran.
In a post on X, Baghaei recalled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s remarks during Israel’s June 2025 military campaign: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
He contrasted those words with German officials’ recent warnings against renewed attacks and calls to prevent further escalation, before citing Friedrich Schiller’s The Maid of Orleans, quoting a passage that portrays reason being helplessly dragged towards an abyss by the forces of madness.
